blocks.text: Most people who search for an AI assistant for VS Code on Mac want help while they stay in the editor. Lazur works that way, but from the outside. It is a voice assistant that lives in the notch of your Mac. You hold a key, ask a question, and Lazur answers out loud. It can point at things on your screen and walk you through steps. This page explains each job with examples, and it shows where the limits are.
Why developers on Mac search for an AI helper in VS Code

VS Code is a common tool for working developers. In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 75.9% of respondents said they use Visual Studio Code. That survey drew more than 49,000 responses from 177 countries. Most respondents in that survey use it, so the same questions come up again and again.

Microsoft also reports a wider number. It says 50 million developers use Visual Studio and Visual Studio Code each month. That figure was announced in May 2025, and it combines both products. It is not a VS Code-only count, so treat it as a rough sign of scale.

Your question is usually one of four. What does this message mean? Where is that setting? How do I do this step? Can you write this text for me? Lazur covers all four, with your voice and what is on your screen. Each one maps to a different job, and each job works a little differently.
Lazur sits beside VS Code, not inside it

Lazur is not an extension, plugin, or add-in for VS Code. You do not install it from the editor. It runs as a Mac app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. Keep that in mind before you expect it to behave like a panel inside VS Code.

The split works in your favor. VS Code stays the place where you write code. Lazur helps you understand what you see, find what you need, and get words onto the page. It does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. You still press the keys. Lazur tells you which keys to press and what each step should show.
What you can say while VS Code is open
Lazur has a small set of jobs. Each one starts with a different kind of question. Here is what each job does with VS Code in front of you.

items: Explain: ask what a warning, error, or panel means. Hold ⌥⌘, ask, and let go. Lazur answers out loud.
Point: ask where something is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.
Guide: ask how to do something. Lazur walks you through it one click at a time and waits for each click.
Draft: ask for a piece of text. Lazur drafts it and types it at the cursor.
Dictate: hold fn and talk. Clean, formatted text lands at the cursor in any app.

blocks.text: Explain what is on screen in VS Code

Start here when a message makes no sense. VS Code shows warnings and errors in several places. A red squiggle in the editor, a line in the Problems panel, or a line in the terminal can all confuse you. Hold ⌥⌘, ask your question, and let go. Lazur answers out loud from what it can see.

Ask a narrow question. 'What does this mean?' gets a general answer. 'What does this warning mean in this file?' gets a useful one. Lazur answers from the screen it sees, so the words on that screen matter. If the message scrolls away, hold the key again while the text is still visible.
Follow up with a second question. Ask 'where do I look next?' and Lazur points at the line, panel, or menu that matters. You then decide what to change. Lazur does not make the change for you.

blocks.title: Ask about the screen you have
blocks.text: Lazur sees what is on screen when you hold the key. It does not read your whole project. Open the file or panel you care about first, then ask.
Point at a button and guide me through a feature

Pointing and guiding look similar, but they answer different questions. A point answers where. A guide answers how. Ask 'where is the Keyboard Shortcuts editor?' and Lazur draws a circle and a label around the place on your screen. Ask 'how do I change a shortcut?' and Lazur walks you through it one step at a time.
The guide waits. Lazur gives one step, then waits for you to do it before it gives the next. That feels slow at first. It also stops you from clicking through a menu you did not mean to open.

VS Code's keybindings docs list two short routes to the Keyboard Shortcuts editor. Press ⌘K then ⌘S. Or press ⇧⌘P to open the Command Palette, then run Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts. Either one works. Lazur can point at the Command Palette if you forget the shortcut.

items: Ask Lazur where the Keyboard Shortcuts editor is. Lazur circles it.
Open the editor with ⌘K then ⌘S, or run Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts from the Command Palette.
Search for the command you want to change. Ask Lazur to explain any column you do not recognize.
Change the key, then check the result in the editor before you close the window.

blocks.text: The common mistake is asking for the whole process at once. Ask for the first step. Then ask for the next one. You keep control of the pace, and you can stop at any point without losing your place.
Dictate and draft text at the cursor

Dictation and drafting are two different tools. Hold fn to dictate. Your words become clean, formatted text at the cursor, in any app. Lazur also has snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots. Use the dictionary for names that speech recognition gets wrong, such as function names, library names, or a teammate's name.

Drafting works differently. You ask for content, and Lazur writes it. It types the draft at the cursor. You read the text and keep what works. A commit message makes a good test. Put the cursor in your message box and ask for a short draft based on the change on screen. Read every line. Lazur does not run Git or commit for you.

blocks.title: Drafts look right, even when they are wrong
blocks.text: In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, 66% named AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite, as their top frustration. These figures cover AI tools in general, not VS Code. Read every draft before you use it.
Common VS Code on Mac problems and how Lazur helps

The official Visual Studio Code FAQ does not publish a list of its most visited topics. Its troubleshooting headings are the closest signal. They name four problems that people run into on Mac and other systems. Each one is a place where a spoken helper can save you a few minutes of searching.

items: Resolving shell environment fails. Lazur can explain the error on screen and guide you through the checks in the FAQ. It does not change your shell files for you.
Investigate slow shell initialization. This is about how long your terminal takes to start. Lazur can point at the startup output you see and explain it. The fix stays with you.
VS Code gets unresponsive right after opening a folder. Ask Lazur to guide you through the steps one at a time. Note what happened just before the freeze, because that detail helps.
VS Code is blank. Lazur can help you describe what you see, then guide you through the FAQ steps. It cannot see a window you have not opened.

blocks.text: A word of caution. These headings show topics the FAQ covers. They do not show how often people search for each one. Treat the list as a map of common trouble spots, not a ranking of searches.
Check your Mac before you install VS Code

Check your macOS version before you download anything. The Mac Universal build of VS Code requires macOS 12.0 or later. The download is under 200 MB, and the installed footprint is under 500 MB. Plan for both numbers, especially on a Mac with little free space.

VS Code follows Apple's security update window. That usually means the latest macOS release plus the two previous versions. Older systems fall outside that window. VS Code deprecated support for Big Sur, macOS 11.0 and older, starting with version 1.105 in September 2025. It stopped updating Big Sur from version 1.107 in November 2025. The last release for Big Sur is 1.106.

blocks.text: Some listings online give macOS 11 as the minimum. The official download page says macOS 12.0 or later. Use the official number when you plan an install. If you are on Big Sur, the FAQ points to Apple's support site for the upgrade steps.
Which VS Code release is current

The current stable release is Visual Studio Code 1.145, dated November 4, 2026. Its headline items include Remote agents in Preview, Automations with cron expressions, and experimental agent verbosity modes. These are the notes to read if you want to know what changed.

The 1.145 notes list no macOS-specific changes and no keyboard shortcut changes. So the shortcuts in this page should still apply on that release. The download page does not show a version number, so compare your installed build with the release notes when you need to confirm.

blocks.title: Ask again after an update
blocks.text: Lazur answers from what is on screen. If a menu looks different after an update, ask again with the new screen in view. Old answers may describe the old layout.
Mistakes people make with an AI helper in VS Code

items: Expecting Lazur to click. It points and guides. You do the clicking.
Searching the VS Code marketplace for it. Lazur is a Mac app, not an extension.
Asking vague questions. Name the file, panel, or message you mean.
Holding the key after the error has gone. Hold it while the text is visible.
Dictating code names without adding them to the personal dictionary. Speech recognition guesses, and a wrong guess can look right.
Accepting a draft without reading it. Read it, then edit it.
Holding the key with secrets on screen. Close the file or hide the terminal first.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes share one habit. You treat the answer as finished. Treat it as a first draft of help. Ask a follow-up, check the screen, and then decide.
Privacy when Lazur sees your screen

Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. When you hold ⌥⌘, the audio and a screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer. Those are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, and that memory stays on your Mac.

Think about what is on screen before you hold the key. A terminal with a token, a .env file, or a client's private code can all appear in the screenshot. Close or hide those windows first. This is a habit, not a setting. Lazur cannot tell which text is sensitive. You can.
Keyboard shortcuts to learn alongside Lazur

A few VS Code shortcuts make Lazur's steps faster to follow. Lazur itself uses two keys on the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask. Hold fn to dictate. The VS Code shortcuts below come from the official keybindings docs.

items: ⇧⌘P opens the Command Palette. Most commands start here.
⌘K then ⌘S opens the Keyboard Shortcuts editor.
⌘/ toggles a line comment in the editor.
Help > Keyboard Shortcut Reference opens a condensed PDF for printing. Pick the macOS version, which is laid out for a US English keyboard.

blocks.title: Print the reference and keep it close
blocks.text: Print the Keyboard Shortcut Reference and keep it beside your keyboard. Ask Lazur about any key you do not recognize, and it will explain what it sees.
Who this fits, and who should look elsewhere

Lazur fits you if you work on a Mac, want spoken answers, and switch between VS Code, the browser, and your notes. It also fits people who think better out loud. Dictation at the cursor helps with commit messages, comments, and pull request text.

Look elsewhere if you need Windows. Windows is planned, not available. Look elsewhere if you need a tool that writes code into your project files. Lazur does not edit files. Also look elsewhere if you want suggestions that appear as you type. Lazur is a voice assistant. Its strength is what you can ask and what you can see.
Next steps for VS Code on Mac

Start with one question about one thing on your screen. Hold ⌥⌘, ask, and listen. Then try one guided task, such as the Keyboard Shortcuts editor. When you are ready, [download Lazur for Mac](/download). You can read the [plans on the pricing page](/pricing) before you decide.

If you use VS Code every day, the [VS Code for developers on Mac](/for/developers/vs-code) guide covers setup, shortcuts, debugging, and Git. If you want to see how fast you type compared with how fast you talk, try the [typing speed test](/tools/typing-speed-test).

faq.question: Is Lazur an extension for VS Code?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It is not a plugin, extension, or add-in for VS Code, and it has no partnership with any app maker. You use it alongside the editor, not inside it.

faq.question: Can Lazur write code into my project files?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and dictates text at the cursor. It does not edit files or operate other apps for you. You read the text and keep what works.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Windows is planned, not available. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

faq.question: Which macOS version does VS Code need?
faq.answer: The Mac Universal build of VS Code requires macOS 12.0 or later. VS Code supports the latest macOS release and the two previous versions. Big Sur, macOS 11.0 and older, got its last update in version 1.106.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Is my code used to train AI models?
faq.answer: Lazur says content is never used to train AI models. The memory of what you asked and did stays on your Mac.

faq.question: Can Lazur fix a shell environment error for me?
faq.answer: It can explain the error on screen and guide you through the checks, one step at a time. It does not change your shell files for you. You make the change yourself.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur has a Pro trial, and no credit card is needed. The trial starts when you first open the app.

faq.question: Where do I find the VS Code keyboard shortcuts?
faq.answer: Press ⌘K then ⌘S to open the Keyboard Shortcuts editor. Or press ⇧⌘P and run Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts. The Help menu also has a Keyboard Shortcut Reference PDF.
